vignette:
Mark, a 39-year-old construction worker, had always believed that hard work and resilience would shield him from life's darker realities. But everything changed one fateful afternoon at a job site, a place he had frequented for years. As he was helping his crew dismantle a series of scaffolds, a sudden collapse sent a fellow worker plummeting to the ground. Mark's heart raced as he watched helplessly, the gruesome sight searing into his mind. The cries of his colleague echoed in the air, and even now, years later, Mark could still picture the moment vividly-the way the sunlight glinted off the metal beams just before they gave way, the smell of dust and sweat mingling with the copper tang of blood. This memory had become a part of him, a relentless specter that haunted his daily life.

In the months following the incident, Mark tried to push away his feelings, convinced that expressing anger or grief would only make things worse. "What good would it do to feel angry?" he would think. "It won't change what happened." Instead, he buried his emotions deep, even when they clawed at him from the inside. He had come to believe that if he didn't acknowledge the pain, it would eventually fade away. But that wasn't the case. The anger he suppressed morphed into a dull ache of inadequacy, a nagging sense that he had failed-not just his colleague, but himself. The world felt unsafe, unpredictable, and Mark was certain that he was powerless to stop bad things from happening. This belief twisted like a knife in his gut, reinforcing his feelings of helplessness.

Avoidance became his default strategy. Mark stopped going to the construction site he had worked at for over a decade, opting instead for odd jobs that kept him away from the chaos of heavy machinery and high places. The job site was a constant reminder of his trauma, and he could not bear to face it. In his downtime, he sought distractions in the form of gambling. It became a way to escape the memories that plagued him-each spin of the roulette wheel a temporary reprieve from the images that flooded his mind. Yet, what he sought as a thrill only deepened his despair. The fleeting excitement of gambling never filled the void left by that day, and he often found himself losing more than he could afford, both financially and emotionally.

As time passed, Mark's coping mechanisms grew increasingly maladaptive. He found himself dissociating deliberately, trying to escape from his own body when the memories became overwhelming. It started with brief moments of zoning out during conversations, but eventually escalated to longer episodes where he would simply drift away, blanking out the reality around him. He could taste the dust from the construction site in the back of his throat during these episodes, a stark reminder of what he tried to forget. Mark felt trapped in a cycle of avoidance, unable to confront the memories that held him captive while simultaneously feeling like he was losing himself in the process.

His relationships began to suffer as well. Friends and family noticed his withdrawal, but Mark brushed off their concerns with the practiced ease of someone who had grown accustomed to hiding his pain. He would smile and nod, assuring them he was fine, but inside, he felt increasingly isolated. His ex-wife, once a source of support, drifted further away as she struggled to understand the man he had become. Mark could see the disappointment in her eyes, and it crushed him. He felt inadequate not just as a worker but as a husband and father, convinced that he was letting everyone down. 

Finally, after years of battling these demons alone, Mark reached a breaking point. A recent incident at a construction site-a young worker falling and narrowly avoiding disaster-triggered a flood of emotions he could no longer suppress. The images of his colleague's fall rushed back with a ferocity that left him gasping. It was the first time in years he had allowed himself to feel anything close to fear, and it terrified him. He realized he could not continue living in this state of perpetual avoidance and despair. 

Sitting in his truck that day, Mark made the decision to seek help. What frightened him most was the thought of facing those memories head-on and the possibility that he might never fully escape the shadows of that day. But he also hoped that perhaps, with guidance, he could learn to reclaim his life and restore some sense of normalcy. As he sat in the driver's seat, the weight of his decision hung heavy in the air, but there was a flicker of hope-maybe, just maybe, this was the beginning of a different journey.
